Performance outcome

The rider runs practice like an experiment: a baseline run, then one change at a time, judged with video, section splits and notes, rather than by feel or one fast lap.

Who it’s for

Competitive riders, and any advanced rider who wants practice time to produce real improvement.

Before this lesson

  • Race Track Walk.
  • Access to a camera; timing equipment where available.

Why it matters

Riders often feel fastest when they are not. Video and timing turn practice into evidence, and testing one change at a time shows what actually works.

Technical model

Source check: d01 (video only: not yet watched), d13 (could not be opened). The reviewer must confirm this section against the original.

Baseline first

Start with a normal run to compare against.

One change at a time

Change a line, a brake marker or a setup setting, but only one thing, so the result can be attributed to it.

Record everything

Conditions, tyre and suspension changes, fatigue, line changes and what the run was for. Without notes, results can’t be compared.

Feel versus evidence

Compare what the rider felt with video and splits. They often disagree, and that disagreement is useful.

Know the limits of the data

Phone GPS, action-camera timestamps and stopwatches are noisy. Small differences may not be real.

Physics & maths

Signal, noise and one fast run

Every run varies. To tell whether a change helped, compare several runs before and after: their averages and their spread. If the difference between averages is small compared with the spread, the change may not have made a real difference. One faster run is not proof.

A good Mathlete visual: split times before and after a change, with the noise band shown. This lesson connects directly to statistics.

Common errors

What you seePossible causesCorrection
Changing several things at once.Impatience; limited practice time.Coach to supply
Trusting one fast run.Not comparing averages and spread.Coach to supply
No notes, so results can’t be compared later.No system for recording.Coach to supply

Practice design

Setting
A practice session on a known track or section, with a camera and timing if available.
Focus
Baseline, one change, compare.
Feedback
Lap log: date, track, conditions, setup, line notes, times and splits.

Stop when

  • Fatigue makes later runs incomparable.
  • Conditions change during the session.

Video analysis

What the rider and coach look for in footage:

  • Was there a baseline?
  • Was only one thing changed per test?
  • Were conditions and setup recorded?
  • Is the conclusion supported by more than one run?

Ready to move on

  • The rider runs a session with a baseline and one tested change, and reports a conclusion the coach agrees the data supports.

Educational checkpoints, not safety certificates.

Safety

Class 2: advanced riding skills. Needs the stated prerequisites, a controlled progression, suitable terrain and coaching guidance.

Practice only on terrain your coach has chosen, within your current skill, with the right protective equipment. Completing a lesson isn’t a safety certificate and doesn’t mean a rider is ready to try anything.
